name: Martin Luther King Jr.
role: Baptist minister and civil rights leader; SCLC president (1957-1968)
summary: King led the nonviolent civil rights movement against segregation, grounding civil disobedience in a higher moral law. In his last years he extended his aims to economic justice, calling for a guaranteed income, jobs and a restructuring of American society, and opposed the Vietnam War. He rejected both communism and laissez-faire capitalism and favored a synthesis of the two.

unions-good.rationale: Led support for the 1968 Memphis sanitation workers' strike and, in 1967, held up a labor union's power to make a corporation say yes as an example of power used well.

cut-welfare.rationale: Argued that a guaranteed income would raise dignity and self-improvement, and noted that early objections that it would destroy initiative were outdated; he wanted economic security expanded, not cut.

basic-income.rationale: Called for a guaranteed annual income, 'a guaranteed minimum income for all people', and urged the movement to organize for it; he paired it with full employment and cited estimates that it was affordable.

job-guarantee.rationale: Said the movement was now struggling to 'guarantee a livable income and a good solid job' and that the nation must 'create full employment, or create incomes'.

priority-to-poor.rationale: Built his last campaign around the poor and said a nation spending more on military defense than on social uplift is 'approaching spiritual death'.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Named 'extreme materialism' one of the 'giant triplets' that must be overcome and said it is a problem when profit motives and property rights are valued above people.

property-fundamental.rationale: Said that when 'profit motives and property rights are considered more important than people' the social evils cannot be conquered, which rejects treating property as an overriding right.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Same Riverside Church passage ranks people above property rights and profit motives; he also asked who owns the oil and iron ore.

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: 1967: 'communism forgets that life is individual. Capitalism forgets that life is social,' with brotherhood found in 'a higher synthesis' of both; he rejected dialectical materialism.

defeat-communism.rationale: He rejected Marxism and called communism a danger, but said it will not be defeated by bombs or war and should be countered by a 'positive thrust for democracy' and justice. Evidence points both ways.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: Rejected Marx's 'dialectical materialism' and a 'materialistic interpretation of history', stressing idealism and spiritual values.

religion-illusion.rationale: Rejected communism partly because it denied religion; he was a minister who held that human life has a spiritual dimension.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Criticised Marx for dropping 'idealism and spiritualism' and framed the struggle as moral and religious, with materialism named as an evil.

one-party-rule.rationale: Cited the 'political totalitarianism' of communism as a reason for rejecting it.

political-violence-never.rationale: Said riots are 'socially destructive and self-defeating', that violence creates more problems than it solves and that nonviolence is the most potent weapon; he also urged nonviolence between nations. Early in his career he had guns for self-defense and he later tolerated armed protectors, so the claim is 'never' only as to his own movement.

means-match-ends.rationale: 'Nonviolence demands that the means we use must be as pure as the ends we seek'; it is wrong to use immoral means to attain moral ends.

unjust-law-not-binding.rationale: Quoted St. Augustine that 'an unjust law is no law at all' and argued one has a moral responsibility to disobey unjust laws.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: Said there is a moral responsibility to obey just laws and to disobey unjust ones, so the duty depends on a law's justice, not on its being law; he was clear that breakers must act openly and accept the penalty.

revolution-justified.rationale: Called a violent revolution impracticable and counterproductive for Black Americans and sought a nonviolent 'revolution of values', while warning that those who make peaceful revolution impossible make violent revolution inevitable.

direct-action.rationale: Led nonviolent direct action (sit-ins, marches, boycotts), but also campaigned for voter registration and the Voting Rights Act, so he did not set action against elections.

democracy-best.rationale: Said the best defense against communism is a 'positive thrust for democracy' and that the sit-ins sought the 'wells of democracy' of the founding documents.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Argued a law is unjust if imposed on a minority that, denied the vote, had no part in enacting it.

racial-franchise.rationale: Campaigned for Black voting rights; called laws made without minority voters unjust and backed the Voting Rights Act.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Held that segregation 'relegates persons to the status of things' and that all people are of infinite worth, made in the image of God; the Dream speech affirms that all are created equal.

more-religion-public.rationale: Expected the church to take part in public moral struggles and criticised its silence, while himself leading as a minister.

universal-morality.rationale: Grounded just law in 'the moral law or the law of God', citing Aquinas on eternal and natural law as the test of all human law.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Called all segregation statutes unjust and morally wrong, and urged people to disobey segregation ordinances.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: Said slavery and discrimination put Black Americans far behind; he proposed a government compensatory program of $50 billion over ten years for disadvantaged groups (Playboy, 1965).

racism-not-main-obstacle.rationale: In 1967 called racism one of three 'interrelated' evils and described continuing gaps in jobs, housing and schooling.

gradual-change.rationale: Rejected 'Wait', which he said 'has almost always meant Never', and criticised the white moderate's counsel of patience.

freedom-to-discriminate.rationale: Led sit-ins at privately owned lunch counters and boycotts of businesses refusing jobs ('If you respect my dollar, you must respect my person').

empower-police-military.rationale: Criticised spending on military defense above social uplift and condemned police brutality in Birmingham.

war-builds-character.rationale: Said war cannot be reconciled with wisdom, justice and love, pointing to napalm, orphans and deranged veterans; he called for a world beyond war.

arms-reduction.rationale: Nobel lecture called for study of nonviolence between nations and for the will to achieve disarmament and peace; Beyond Vietnam warned against nuclear war.

national-self-determination.rationale: Criticised the US for rejecting 'a revolutionary government seeking self-determination' in Vietnam.

land-redistribution.rationale: Said land reform was among the Vietnamese peasants' most important needs and condemned US alliance with the landed gentry of Latin America.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: Nobel lecture: 'The wealthy nations must go all out to bridge the gulf between the rich minority and the poor majority.'

world-economy-extracts-surplus.rationale: Said Western capitalists invest in Asia, Africa and South America 'only to take the profits out with no concern for the social betterment of the countries', calling this unjust; he did not give a structural theory.

positive-liberty.rationale: Linked freedom to material security, saying a guaranteed income would let people make decisions about their lives, and that economic power was needed for real freedom.

participatory-democracy.rationale: Condemned the powerlessness of people 'stripped of the right to make decisions concerning his life and destiny' and organized communities for economic and political power.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Inferred: he urged obedience to the 1954 Supreme Court decision and disobedience to majority-enacted segregation ordinances, which treats courts as a legitimate check on majorities.
